'''John William Wrench, Jr.''' (October 13, 1911 – February 27, 2009) was an [[Americans|American]] [[mathematician]] who worked primarily in [[numerical analysis]]. He was a pioneer in using [[computer]]s for mathematical calculations, and is noted for work done with [[Daniel Shanks]] to calculate the [[mathematical constant]] [[pi]] to 100,000 decimal places.

==Life and education==
Wrench was born on October 13, 1911, in [[Westfield, New York]], and grew up in [[Hamburg, New York]]. He received a [[Bachelor of Arts|BA]] [[summa cum laude]] in [[mathematics]] in 1933 and an [[Master of Arts|MA]] in mathematics in 1935, both from the [[University at Buffalo]]. He received his [[PhD]] in mathematics in 1938 from [[Yale University]].<ref name="NP obit">
{{cite news|title=Obituary: Dr. John Wrench Jr. |url=http://www.fredericknewspost.com/sections/local/obit_detail.htm?obitID=25989 |work=Frederick News-Post |location=Frederick, Maryland |date=March 20, 2009 |accessdate=21 April 2009 |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20120229084005/http://www.fredericknewspost.com/sections/local/obit_detail.htm?obitID=25989 |archivedate=29 February 2012 |url-status=dead }}
</ref>
His thesis was titled ''The derivation of arctangent relations''.<ref>
{{cite journal |date=May 1939 |title=Notes |journal=Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society |volume=45 |issue=5 |pages=349–354 |publisher=American Mathematical Society |location=Providence, RI |issn=0273-0979|url=https://www.ams.org/bull/1939-45-05/S0002-9904-1939-06990-5/S0002-9904-1939-06990-5.pdf |accessdate=2009-04-19 |doi=10.1090/S0002-9904-1939-06990-5 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

Wrench died on February 27, 2009, of [[pneumonia]] in [[Frederick, Maryland]].<ref name="WashPost obit">
{{cite news|first=Matt |last=Schudel |title=Mathematician Had a Taste for Pi |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2009/03/24/AR2009032403064_pf.html |newspaper=Washington Post |page=B05 |date=March 25, 2009 |accessdate=31 March 2009 |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20121108232728/http://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2009/03/24/AR2009032403064_pf.html |archivedate=8 November 2012 |url-status=dead }}
</ref>

==Career==
Wrench started his career teaching at [[George Washington University]], but switched to doing research for the [[United States Navy]] during [[World War II]]. His specialty for the Navy was developing high-speed computational methods, and he was a pioneer in using computers for mathematical calculations. He worked on projects involving [[Underwater acoustics|underwater sound waves]], [[underwater explosion]]s, [[structural design]], [[hydrodynamics]], [[aerodynamics]], and [[data analysis]]. He became deputy head of the Applied Mathematics Laboratory at the Navy's [[David Taylor Model Basin]] in 1953, and retired in 1974 as the head of the laboratory. He also had academic appointments at [[Yale University]], [[Wesleyan University]], [[University of Maryland, College Park]], and [[American University]].<ref name="WashPost obit" />

Wrench had a particular interest in computing the decimal digits of [[Pi|π]], and performed some lengthy calculations even before the availability of computers.<ref name="WashPost obit" /> During the period 1945–1956 Wrench and Levi B. Smith used a [[Mechanical calculator|desk calculator]] to produce more and more digits of π, ending with 1160 places.<ref>
{{cite journal |last=Wrench, Jr. |first=John W. |date=December 1960|title=The evolution of extended decimal approximations to π |journal=The Mathematics Teacher |volume=53 |pages=644–650|doi=10.5951/MT.53.8.0644 }}
</ref>
In 1961, Wrench and [[Daniel Shanks]] used an [[IBM 7090]] computer to calculate π to 100,000 digits.<ref>
{{cite journal
 | last = Shanks
 | first = Daniel
 | authorlink=Daniel Shanks
 |author2=John W. Wrench Jr
 | year = 1962
 | title = Calculation of π to 100,000 Decimals
 | journal = Mathematics of Computation
 | volume = 16
 | pages = 76–99
 | issn = 0025-5718
 | doi = 10.2307/2003813
 | issue =77
 | quote =
 
 | publisher = American Mathematical Society
 | jstor = 2003813
 }}
</ref>
Harry Polachek had a printout of the 100,000 digits specially bound, inscribed in gold letters, and donated to the [[Smithsonian Institution]].<ref>
{{cite journal |last=Polachek |first=Harry |editor=James Tomayko |year=1996 |title=Anecdotes: Computers vs. the Human Race |url=https://priorart.ip.com/IPCOM/000129969/ |accessdate=2020-07-23 |journal=IEEE Annals of the History of Computing |volume=18 |issue=4 |page=60 |publisher=Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers |issn=1058-6180 |quote=In order to assure the preservation of this document, I arranged for two clear copies of the output to be printed and specially bound (inscribed in gold letters)—one of which I donated to the Smithsonian Institution in Washington, D.C.; the other I kept. The transfer to the Smithsonian took place at a small ceremony, attended by about 25 invited guests. |doi=10.1109/mahc.1996.539917|s2cid=11763917 |url-access=subscription }}
</ref>

Wrench also calculated a number of other [[mathematical constant]]s to high precision, for example the [[Euler–Mascheroni constant]] γ to 328 decimal places<ref>
{{cite journal |last=Wrench, Jr. |first=J. W. |year=1952 |title=A new calculation of Euler's constant |journal=Mathematical Tables and Other Aids to Computation |volume=6 |pages=255 }}
</ref>
and [[Khinchin's constant]] to 65 places.<ref>
{{cite journal |last=Shanks |first=Daniel |authorlink=Daniel Shanks |author2=J. W. Wrench Jr |date=April 1959 |title=Khintchine's Constant |journal=American Mathematical Monthly |volume=66 |issue=5 |pages=276–279 |doi=10.2307/2309633 |publisher=Mathematical Association of America |jstor=2309633 }}
</ref>

He was the editor of the ''Journal of Mathematics of Computation'' from 1959 to 1978.<ref name="EditorialBoard">{{cite web | title=Mathematics of Computation :: Past Editorial Board Members | website=American Mathematical Society | date=2024-07-15 | url=https://www.ams.org/publications/journals/journalsframework/mcom/editorial_history_mcom | access-date=2025-05-15}}</ref> Wrench was a member of the [[National Academy of Sciences]] and the [[United States National Research Council|National Research Council]]. He published more than 150 scientific papers.
